newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey, Gazprom sign $13.5 billion natural gas deal.
newsitem.headline: Turkey, Gazprom sign $13.5 billion natural gas deal.

text.p: Turkey on Monday signed a landmark $13.5 billion agreement with Russia'a gas giant Gazprom to get natural gas over 25 years from 1997, senior Turkish officials said.

"The total value of the project is about $13.5 billion and it is a 25-year agreement starting from this year," Mustafa Murathan, head of Turkey's state pipeline concern Botas, told reporters after signing the deal with Gazprom head Rem Vyahirev in Istanbul.
Vyahirev said the deal would enable Turkey to tap Russian gas, presently at six billion cubic metres (bcm) annually, at gradually increasing amounts that will reach 30 bcm by 2010.

"This is final stage of the big project that we have begun sometime ago. The sums involved in this agreement are really big sums. We are going to increase the present six bcm to 30 bcm by 2010," he told reporters.
Turkey's Energy Minister Recai Kutan told the signing ceremony that Turkey's gas need would shoot up to 27 bcm annually by 2000 and to 60 bcm by 2010.
"We have to take urgent measures in 1997, 1998 and 1999 to meet the rising gas demand," he said. The first increase of Russian gas would be by 500 million bcm this year, he said.
He said two companies had been set up by partners including Botas and Gazprom to distrubute the Russian gas in Turkey and to construct an additional pipeline network from Russia to Turkey.
No further details were immediately available.
Turkey and Russia have been discussing the details of the project since mid-1996.

The project suggested a capacity rise in the existing western pipeline through Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria to 14 bcm from six bmc annually and building another line in the east thgrough Georgia with an annual capacity of 16 bmc.

But Gazprom later suggested an alternative 440-km (275-mile) line that will originate from Izobilnoye port in southern Russia to reach Turkey's Samsun Black Sea port. It will later come to Ankara from Samsun through another 400 km pipeline.
Officials said the underwater pipeline could cost around $3.3 billion.
Turkish officials said earlier the plan to lay another line through Georgia had not been shelved and it was still under consideration.

Turkey wants to diversify its energy resources and looks to various gas suppliers to lessen dependence on oil and coal. Energy demands grow at about 12 percent a year and Turkish officials have for some time been warning of a severe energy shortfall if no measures are taken.
The government has invited tenders for the first nuclear power plant in the country to be built on the southern coastal village of Akkuyu in Mersin province. It will announce the bidders on June 30.
Turkey currently uses about 57 percent of its gas imports to produce electricity.

Its giant agreement with Iran to get gas through a pipeline under a $23-billion deal for 23 years from 1998 is underway. Under this deal Turkey will receive three bcm from 1988 and the amount will be increased to 10 bcm from 2005.
Kutan, asked about U.S. criticism of the agreement with the Islamic state, said Turkey had no choice but to deal with Iran if it was to meet its natural gas needs.
"Our natural gas needs may well reach 60 bcm by 2010. What we can obtain from Russia is about 30 bcm...so we must get the other 30 bcm from elsewhere," he said.
"We explained to them (the United States) that it was imperative we get natural gas from Iran."

He added that work was underway to build two liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals in the Turkish ports of Iskenderun and Izmir, which would receive LNG from Egypt, Yemen and Nigeria. This would help meet Turkey's 2000 needs of 27 bcm, he said.
